## What happens when you render {#how-a-document-becomes-a-document}

![](pics/tools/render-pipeline.png){fig-align="center" width="62%" fig-alt="A diagram of rendering: a qmd file goes to knitr, which writes a md file, which pandoc turns into a Word document, a PDF or a web page."}

::: {.small .fs-80}
You write **one** source file. Rendering runs its code, puts the results in place, and produces whatever output you asked for from that one source. An error in a chunk stops the render, and Quarto names the chunk at which it stopped.
:::

::: notes
You write one source file, with prose and code together. When you render it, knitr, or Jupyter if you work in Python, hands every chunk to R in a fresh session, collects whatever comes back and writes a plain Markdown file with the results placed after the code that produced them. Pandoc, a document converter, then turns that file into whatever you asked for, a Word document for a co-author, a PDF for a journal, a web page for a project, or slides like these. A number is therefore computed in one place, and every output shows the same number. Because the code runs before any typesetting, an error in a chunk halts the render and no new output appears, and Quarto names the chunk that failed, which is the first reason to give every chunk a label.
:::
